title: AI and the New Age of Bioweapons
gist: Former White House Homeland Security Adviser Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall argues that AI has collapsed the barriers to engineering dangerous pathogens — large language models now outperform PhD virologists on lab-relevant knowledge tests — making Cold War-style nuclear deterrence against biological attack obsolete, and calls for a 'deterrence by resilience' strategy built on nationwide pathogen monitoring, critical-infrastructure status for biotech, a strategic biomanufacturing reserve, and reduced U.S. biotech dependency on China.

themes.theme: AI has collapsed the technical barrier to bioweapons

insights.claim: By April 2025, university and nonprofit researchers found that large language models consistently outperformed PhD-level virologists on tests of the knowledge needed to conduct laboratory experiments — a dramatic reversal from just three years earlier, when large language models failed simple biology tests.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated benchmark (April 2025) showing frontier AI models have crossed a critical 'uplift' threshold in virology expertise, directly relevant to AI-safety policy timing and biosecurity regulatory urgency.
insights.quote: Three years ago, large language models failed simple biology tests. But by April 2025, a group of university and nonprofit researchers found that large language models consistently outperformed Ph.D.-level virologists on tests of the knowledge needed to conduct laboratory experiments.

insights.claim: A terrorist group with minimal skills could, in the foreseeable future, use a jailbroken AI model trained on comprehensive biological data to design a more lethal, more transmissible strain of H5N1 avian influenza, then anonymously contract a 'cloud lab' to build and test the virus and a biomanufacturer to produce it at scale, entirely without regulatory oversight.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Describes a concrete, currently-unregulated attack pathway (jailbroken model + contract cloud lab + contract biomanufacturer) that lowers the resource and skill bar for a catastrophic biological attack to near zero — a scenario planning benchmark for biosecurity and biotech-regulation investors.
insights.quote: In the foreseeable future, a terrorist group with minimal skills could access a jailbroken AI model (one that has evaded safety controls) trained on the world’s most comprehensive biological data set... Right now, there are no regulations governing any of this activity.
insights.locator: opening scenario / 'Science Fiction to Science Fact' section

insights.claim: 'Cloud labs' — contract-for-service facilities that can receive digital orders, design and execute experiments, and evaluate outcomes with increasing automation and robotics — combined with specialized contract biomanufacturers, currently operate with no regulations governing their activity.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named, currently unregulated commercial infrastructure layer (cloud labs + contract biomanufacturers) as the critical enabling chokepoint for AI-enabled bioweapons — a clear target for near-term biosecurity regulation and a watch item for the cloud-lab industry itself.
insights.quote: the advent of “cloud labs,” which can receive digital orders, design and execute experiments based on them, and evaluate the outcomes, combined with specialized contract manufacturers that provide biotech production services. Right now, there are no regulations governing any of this activity.

themes.theme: Why nuclear-style deterrence no longer works against bio threats

insights.claim: For decades, U.S. deterrence against biological attack relied on threatening nuclear retaliation against a small number of state actors capable of developing the most dangerous bioweapons — a strategy that no longer works now that AI allows a far broader range of actors, including terrorist groups and even individuals, to develop bioweapons of their own.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: States plainly that the foundational U.S. bio-deterrence doctrine is now obsolete, which should reframe expectations for how quickly a new bio-deterrence and biosecurity regulatory regime needs to be built.
insights.quote: Yet that strategy was effective because only a small number of governments were developing the most dangerous biological weapons. It no longer works in a world in which AI allows more actors—rogue states, terrorist groups, even individuals—to develop new bioweapons of their own.

insights.claim: The bio-risk club is already larger than the nuclear club and will inevitably grow much larger, because biological building blocks are dual-use technologies with immense civilian upside that cannot be locked down in government-controlled facilities the way fissile nuclear materials can.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Explains structurally why bio-proliferation control is a fundamentally harder problem than nuclear nonproliferation — dual-use civilian value makes containment infeasible — directly relevant to any regulatory or investment thesis on biosecurity screening technology.
insights.quote: the bio-risk club is already large and will inevitably become much larger than the nuclear club... because the building blocks of biological threats are most often dual-use technologies and because they have immense upside, it is not possible to fully prevent the generation of potentially harmful materials
insights.locator: 'Brave New World' section, four reasons deterrence-by-punishment fails

insights.claim: Because AI-enabled biotechnology is deeply embedded in the economies of U.S. allies and partners, Washington cannot offer 'extended deterrence' (protection in exchange for forbearance) the way it has with its nuclear umbrella, since the economic benefits of bioconvergence matter too much to allies' own well-being.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural limit on U.S. ability to lead a coordinated allied biosecurity regime, since allies have independent economic incentives to develop bioconvergence capability rather than accept U.S.-controlled restraint.
insights.quote: given the role that AI-enabled biotechnologies already play in multiple sectors of the economies of Washington’s allies and partners, extended deterrence will not be plausible.
insights.locator: 'Brave New World' section, four reasons deterrence-by-punishment fails

insights.claim: In June 2026, the Trump administration abruptly imposed export controls on Mythos and Fable — cutting-edge Anthropic products providing AI capabilities to the United Kingdom and European Union — cutting off all foreign users including allies; the controls were later reversed but are likely to spur allies to accelerate development of domestic AI capabilities to reduce dependence on the United States.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A specific, dated (June 2026) incident of U.S. AI export controls being weaponized against allies, later reversed — a concrete data point showing the fragility of allied dependence on U.S. frontier AI products and a catalyst for allied 'AI sovereignty' investment.
insights.quote: the Trump administration has episodically sought to make it harder for other countries to access and use American frontier AI models, including in June 2026, when it suddenly imposed export controls on Mythos and Fable—cutting-edge Anthropic products that provided AI capabilities to the United Kingdom and the European Union. The controls resulted in an abrupt and total cutoff of access to any foreign user, including allies and U.S.-based individuals. This draconian action was subsequently reversed
insights.locator: 'Brave New World' section, four reasons deterrence-by-punishment fails

themes.theme: The 2024 H5N1 outbreak as a preview of systemic gaps

insights.claim: In 2024, naturally occurring H5N1 bird flu spread from poultry to dairy and beef herds and eventually infected more than 70 humans; as the White House homeland security adviser coordinating the federal response, the author found considerable weaknesses in U.S. prevention, monitoring, attribution, and response systems even for this non-deliberate outbreak, including hard-to-acquire and incomplete disease data and slow industry mobilization.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A first-hand, named case study (2024 H5N1, 70+ human infections) demonstrating real, current gaps in U.S. biosurveillance and response capacity even absent an intentional attack — a baseline for assessing readiness against a deliberate AI-designed pathogen.
insights.quote: In 2024, H5N1 bird flu spread from poultry to dairy and beef herds and eventually to more than 70 humans. As the White House homeland security adviser at the time, I coordinated the federal response to this potentially catastrophic threat... there were considerable weaknesses and gaps in U.S. prevention, monitoring, attribution, and response systems.

insights.claim: Responding to the 2024 H5N1 outbreak required substantial new federal funding to rapidly develop an mRNA vaccine and divert U.S. pharmaceutical production lines to manufacture it at scale, and even then there would have been inadequate drug supplies for many months.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Quantifies the real-world lag in vaccine surge capacity (months of inadequate drug supply even with emergency funding), directly informing the urgency of the report's call for a pre-negotiated biomanufacturing 'strategic readiness reserve.'
insights.quote: in order to deliver sufficient quantities of human vaccines to protect the American people, we needed to provide substantial new federal funding to rapidly create an mRNA vaccine and divert U.S. pharmaceutical industry production lines to make it at scale, and there would still have been inadequate drug supplies for many months.

insights.claim: The early warning network for international biological threats that the U.S. established and expanded to more than 50 pivotal countries during the Biden administration was largely dismantled by the Trump administration in 2025.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, reversible policy rollback (dismantling of the 50+ country biothreat early-warning network in 2025) that materially weakens global biosurveillance capacity — a concrete near-term policy-reversal target for future administrations or Congress.
insights.quote: The early warning network for international biological threats—akin to the national missile defense early warning system—that the United States established and championed over the last two decades across multiple presidencies, including an expansion to more than 50 pivotal countries during the Biden administration, was largely dismantled by the Trump administration in 2025.

themes.theme: Concrete attack scenarios beyond the H5N1 case

insights.claim: A plausible nation-state scenario involves engineering a stealthy respiratory pathogen whose symptoms do not emerge until six months after infection, releasing it near U.S. military bases while secretly vaccinating the adversary's own population under the guise of a routine flu-shot program, timed to disrupt U.S. military mobilization when the adversary later initiates overt hostilities.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A specific, detailed nation-state attack scenario (delayed-onset pathogen + covert domestic vaccination + timed with kinetic operations) that should inform Pentagon force-readiness and biodefense planning against sophisticated state adversaries.
insights.quote: a technologically sophisticated foreign adversary could leverage AI, biological design systems, and biomanufacturing tools to engineer a stealthy respiratory pathogen. Through advanced bioengineering, the disease’s symptoms might not emerge until six months after infection.

insights.claim: An ideologically motivated domestic terrorist organization could genetically modify a plant pathogen to destroy a staple U.S. crop such as rice, corn, or wheat, rapidly disrupting the domestic food supply and agricultural economy and causing famine in regions dependent on U.S. crop exports.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Extends AI-bio risk beyond human pathogens to agricultural/food-security attack vectors, relevant to agricultural commodity supply-chain risk assessment.
insights.quote: an ideologically motivated American terrorist organization could genetically modify a plant pathogen so that it destroys a key crop such as rice, corn, or wheat in the United States. This would rapidly disrupt domestic food supply and the agricultural economy

insights.claim: Sherwood-Randall calls for the biotechnology industry to be formally designated a 'critical infrastructure' sector (as was done for 16 sectors after 9/11), with a coordinating council including DNA synthesis providers, AI model developers, genomic data platforms, cloud lab operators, and high-containment laboratories that regularly exercises incident response with government, similar to the electricity sector.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A concrete, specific regulatory recommendation (biotech as critical infrastructure with a formal coordinating council) that, if enacted, would materially reshape compliance and information-sharing obligations for DNA synthesis firms, cloud labs, and AI biotech developers.
insights.quote: The biotechnology industry should now be designated as a critical infrastructure sector. As part of this designation, Washington should establish a coordinating council for the biotechnology sector that includes DNA synthesis providers, AI model developers, genomic data platforms, cloud lab operators, and high-containment laboratories.

insights.claim: The U.S. should establish a national strategic readiness reserve for biothreats, modeled on the Civil Reserve Air Fleet, to guarantee emergency federal access to private-sector computing power, laboratory facilities, personnel, and biomanufacturing capacity for a 'warm start' surge in diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Proposes a specific institutional model (Civil Reserve Air Fleet-style pre-negotiated contracts) for biomanufacturing surge capacity — a potential future revenue and contracting opportunity for biotech and CDMO (contract development and manufacturing organization) firms.
insights.quote: the United States should establish a national strategic readiness reserve for handling biothreats. This can be modeled on the Civil Reserve Air Fleet, which enables the federal government to promptly make use of commercial planes and pilots when a military aircraft shortage emerges.

insights.claim: The U.S. federal clinical trials process is described as far too slow and cumbersome to address a biological crisis, already limiting U.S. biotech competitiveness and diverting drug-development activity to China, creating supply-chain dependencies with security implications.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Names the U.S. clinical trials system as a specific, fixable competitiveness bottleneck actively pushing biotech activity toward China — directly relevant to biotech and pharma regulatory-reform investment theses and to assessing U.S.-China biotech competitive positioning.
insights.quote: the United States must fix the federal clinical trials process, which is far too slow and cumbersome to effectively address a biological crisis. This major bottleneck already limits U.S. biotech competitiveness and diverts activity to China

insights.claim: Congress should mandate that DNA synthesis companies screen customers and the genetic sequences they order to prevent malicious actors from abusing the technology, paired with measures to strengthen the broader U.S. biotech innovation sector so the compliance burden doesn't become onerous.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: A specific, near-term legislative recommendation (mandatory DNA synthesis screening) that would directly impact gene-synthesis companies' compliance costs and business models if enacted.
insights.quote: Congress should immediately pass legislation to mandate that DNA synthesis companies screen customers and the sequences they order to prevent malicious actors from abusing this technology

themes.theme: U.S.-China biotech dependency and the Nunn-Lugar precedent

insights.claim: Over the last five years, U.S. companies have become increasingly dependent on China for components used in many U.S.-market drugs and for access to the latest research in therapeutic molecules, while the U.S. pharmaceutical industry is simultaneously acquiring large volumes of Chinese biotech intellectual property and drug rights despite concerns about Chinese IP theft.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Documents a growing, bidirectional U.S.-China biotech entanglement (drug component dependency plus U.S. acquisition of Chinese biotech IP) creating both supply-chain risk and IP-theft exposure — material for pharma supply-chain and China-decoupling investment analysis.
insights.quote: Over the last five years, American companies have become increasingly dependent on China for the components used in many drugs sold in the U.S. market and for access to the latest research in therapeutic molecules that can treat or cure diseases, creating substantial supply chain risks.

insights.claim: Sherwood-Randall recommends Congress pass legislation modeled on the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act to fund U.S. biotech and pharmaceutical competitiveness via subsidies, R&D investment, and tax incentives, paired with a strengthened national security review process for foreign investment in the sector.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Proposes a specific legislative template (a 'CHIPS Act for biotech') that, if pursued, would represent a major new federal biotech industrial-policy program worth tracking for sector-level investment implications.
insights.quote: This bill might be modeled, in part, on the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, which invested hundreds of billions of dollars in research and manufacturing for strategically important sectors.

insights.claim: Sherwood-Randall cites the early-1990s Nunn-Lugar legislation — bipartisan cooperation between Senators Richard Lugar (R-IN) and Sam Nunn (D-GA) to secure and dismantle Soviet nuclear weapons after the USSR's collapse — as the model for the kind of visionary bipartisan action needed today on AI-enabled bioweapons risk.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
insights.so_what: Frames the needed policy response as comparable in scale and bipartisan character to Nunn-Lugar, a useful historical anchor for gauging how large and politically difficult the required legislative effort would be.
insights.quote: In the early 1990s, Indiana Senator Richard Lugar, a Republican, and Georgia Senator Sam Nunn, a Democrat, came together to enact landmark legislation that enabled the United States to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons and fissile materials after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
